text:
The stall’s canvas roof sagged under the weight of its own dyes, the air thick with the scent of crushed spices and damp wool. A vendor’s cry split the murmur of the crowd—a woman hawking striped scarves, her voice pitched against the clatter of copper cups that hung in a spiral from the stall’s pole. I wove between shoulders slick with salt and sweat, my fingers tight around the folded note in my pocket. The pendant at my throat, my mother’s, pressed flat against my sternum like a second pulse. The vendor’s stall wasn’t just a place to trade; it was the city’s tongue, where secrets traveled faster than the gossip in the guildhalls.

Julian had smiled softly the last time he offered his help—disarming, the way his voice had steadied itself against the unexpected, like a hand braced against a wall. That smile had anchored me then. Now, the memory felt like a rope frayed at the edges.

A child darted past, nearly colliding with a tower of drying kelp. The vendor cursed through her teeth, her fingers flying as she restacked the bundles. My pulse hummed in my throat, quick as a startled bird’s. The note burned against my ribs. Passing it here meant risking more than exchange—it meant trusting the wrong set of eyes to see what mattered. But the alternative was worse: letting the truth sit unspoken, letting the silence between us become another kind of lie.

I caught sight of the recipient—a woman with hair the color of wet sand, her posture easy despite the crowded stall. She stood near the back, hands busy rearranging folded linens. My fingers fidgeted with the note, the paper rough under my thumb. The crowd shifted again, a wave of bodies pressing closer. My breath hitched as the woman’s gaze flicked toward me, her eyes sharp as a knife’s edge.

A commotion erupted to my left—a man shouting about a missing purse, his voice raw with accusation. The stall’s owner rounded on him, her hands up like she could physically push the anger back. The distraction was perfect. I slipped through the gap, my shoulder brushing against a stack of clay pots. One wobbled, its painted face staring up at me like a silent witness.

The woman’s fingers stilled as I approached. She didn’t look at me yet, but she knew. I could feel it in the way the air between us tightened, like a bowstring drawn back. The note in my pocket felt heavier than the pendant at my throat. I exhaled, slow and controlled, the way I’d seen Julian do when the world tilted. His fingers had steadied themselves against the parchment once, like they were bracing against me. Now, I was the one steadying myself against the stall.

“You were expecting this,” I said, my voice low enough to stay between us.

She didn’t answer right away. Instead, her hands folded the linen with deliberate care, her movements precise as a ritual. Then, finally, she looked at me. Her eyes were the color of storm-tossed water—calm on the surface, but hiding depths that could drown you. “I was told to keep an eye out for you,” she murmured.

The words landed wrong. My body reacted before my mind could catch up—warmth flooding my face, my fingers tightening around the note. The pendant slipped a half-inch, cold and insistent against my skin. The stall’s scent of spices suddenly tasted like ash. I’d seen that look on my sister’s face the morning the verdict came down. The same quiet certainty. The same unspoken threat beneath the calm.

“Then you know what it says,” I said, the paper whispering as I pulled it from my pocket.

She didn’t take it immediately. Instead, her gaze dropped to my lips, lingering just a second too long. Julian’s focus tell—lingering like he was savoring the words. It sent a shiver down my spine, the kind that made my heels lift half an inch from the ground. The stall’s owner called out, her voice sharp as a blade, and the moment fractured. The woman’s eyes snapped back to mine, and the tenderness in them hardened into something colder.

“You’re too close,” she said, her voice barely audible over the stall’s chaos. “They’re watching.”

My grip on the note faltered. Julian had once told me that love was never free. I’d thought he meant the cost of it, the sacrifice. Now I wondered if he’d meant the price of keeping it hidden.

A shadow moved at the edge of the stall—a figure in a high-collared coat, their face obscured by a hood. The stall’s owner’s shout cut off mid-word. The air thickened, the scents of spices and damp wool turning stale, like something had died in the stall with us.

The woman’s fingers finally closed around the note. She tucked it into her sleeve with a fluid motion that spoke of practice. “Go,” she said. “Before they decide you’re worth more than the truth.”

I didn’t move. The pendant at my throat was ice against my skin, but the note in her sleeve burned like a brand. The stall’s colors blurred into a kaleidoscope of oranges and blues, the noise of the market fading into a dull roar. My body remembered Julian’s hand on my waist, the way his voice had dropped lower than it should. Now, I was standing in a stall that felt suddenly too small, with a truth I couldn’t unload and a woman who knew exactly how dangerous it was.

I swallowed. “Lead the way.”

The pendant didn’t burn anymore. It was ice against my skin. But just as I prepared to step forward, a shadow fell over the chamber, and the air thickened with an unspoken threat. Vow Arbiter Thorne loomed closer, his presence a chilling reminder of the power he wielded. I could feel the weight of his scrutiny, a silent promise that my past would not remain buried for long.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…
